title: SSD-TS: Exploring the potential of linear state space models for diffusion models in time series imputation

problem.claim: Probabilistic time series imputation requires uncertainty estimation and denoising diffusion probabilistic models have been successful for this task.

gap.claim: Existing DDPM-based imputation methods have denoising backbones with high time complexity and architectures that handle time-series dependencies ineffectively.

contributions.claim: The approach uses Mamba as the backbone denoising module for DDPMs.
The approach designs SSM-based blocks for modeling time-series data.
The authors make their datasets and code available.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report state-of-the-art time series imputation results on multiple real-world datasets.

narrative_sequence.summary: Probabilistic time series imputation is used for uncertainty estimation, and DDPMs have performed well on the task.
Current DDPM-based methods face low-time-complexity sequence-modeling limitations in their denoising backbones.
Current denoising architectures handle time-series dependencies ineffectively.
The approach uses Mamba as a DDPM denoising backbone and designs SSM-based blocks for time-series modeling.
The authors report state-of-the-art results on multiple real-world datasets and release datasets and code.

source_observation.claim: The approach combines diffusion-based imputation with a linear state space model backbone and specialized SSM blocks.

interpretation.claim: Separating backbone efficiency from time-series dependency modeling may address distinct limitations in a sequence-imputation pipeline.

application.claim: When adapting diffusion models to long or structured time series, consider low-complexity sequence backbones together with domain-specific dependency blocks.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish which component is responsible for any reported improvement or whether the approach generalizes beyond the evaluated datasets.

unknowns: The abstract does not identify the datasets, baselines, metrics, or quantitative results.
The abstract does not specify the missingness settings, implementation details, or computational complexity.
The abstract does not provide independent verification of the reported state-of-the-art results.
